Verdict: COND — The Path of Deception.
Narrative captures populist persistence but romanticizes institutional conflict.

Integrity: Conditionally Sound (Hypocrisy: 1.8, z: 2)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- Victor Davis Hanson Analysis: COND (0.5, 0.3) — Romanticizes populist resilience.
- Institutional Backlash: FAIL (-0.6, -0.7) — Ignores systemic polarization costs.
Victor Davis Hanson's new book, 'The Counter Revolution,' examines Donald Trump's political resurgence against heavy institutional resistance.

The Bright Side:
Recognizes that political movements tap into genuine voter alienation from traditional party structures.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing historical narrative (WHO/WHY) with systemic institutional stability (HOW/WHERE).

Social Physics Analysis:
Actors exploit genuine voter frustration (Good Preference) to fuel partisan conflict, running a Smart Selfish Maneuver where institutional opposition is projected as pure malice.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Lesser Evil. Systemic polarization breeds further institutional decay.

The Unavoidable Truth: Political movements persist when existing parties fail to serve their constituents.

The Unavoidable Lie: Romanticizing populist comebacks as purely heroic masks deep democratic strain.

Movements outlast individuals because they tap into unresolved structural grievances, not just personal charisma.

How Trumpism Will Outlast Trump

Victor Davis Hanson's latest book, 'The Counter Revolution,' provides a definitive account of Donald Trump's unprecedented political comeback.

Actual Article Body:
Victor Davis Hanson’s latest book, ‘The Counter Revolution,’ provides a definitive account of Donald Trump’s unprecedented political comeback.

Americans love a comeback kid. It’s why we celebrate Muhammad Ali, who, after being stripped of his title and barred from professional boxing in 1967 for refusing the military draft, returned to reclaim the heavyweight championship in 1974 against George Foreman in the “Rumble in the Jungle.” It’s why we honor people such as Robert Downey Jr., who recovered from drug addictions and arrests to become one of the highest-grossing actors of all time. And, as prolific author and historian Victor Davis Hanson shows in his new book The Counter Revolution: The Fall and Rise of Donald Trump and the MAGA Movement, it’s also why so many Americans find President Donald Trump so compelling.

Though American politics has had its fair share of comebacks — Nixon losing the 1960 presidential election only to win it in 1968; Grover Cleveland losing the presidency in 1888 and then regaining in 1892 — none can compare with that of Trump. Abandoned by many of his allies after the January 6 riot and hounded by a long list of investigations that seemed destined to end his career if not bankrupt him, Trump somehow overcame every doubter and waged a political campaign for the ages that ultimately returned him to the White House. Regardless of how it ends, it’s an incredible story, and Hanson deserves credit for giving us the definitive account.

Hanson reminds us that after the results of the November 2020 presidential elections, things looked bleak for Trump. Appointees, both current and former, were competing with each other to prove their disdain for their seemingly ruined president. After the January 6 riots, which were exclusively blamed on Trump even though Nancy Pelosi was on record admitting, “I take responsibility for the security failures of the Capitol that day,” administration officials ran for the doors.

Two days after January 6, Twitter banned Trump “for life” and Facebook followed suit six months later. When Trump tried to switch to the social media app Parler, Amazon, Apple, and Google all removed the app from their app stores. Even the banking industry largely closed its doors — Deutsche Bank announced it would no longer do business with Trump or the Trump Organization; Signature Bank closed two personal accounts held by Trump; and JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America said they would no longer finance future Trump Organization projects. “Popular wisdom held that his political career was over,” writes Hanson.

Between 2021 and 2025, Trump was “targeted in five different courtrooms, facing ninety-one felony charges and some $500 million in combined fines.” In August 2022, the FBI raided his home, making him the only ex-president to enjoy that honor. When he ran for office again, almost half the states made attempts to ban him from the ballot.

The sheer force of anti-Trump activity after 2020 — which included efforts by current and former members of the federal workforce, academia, mainstream media, and senior retired and active-duty members of the U.S. military — is incredible to consider, given, whatever one thinks of the man, his administration left behind a 1.2 percent inflation rate, near record-low peacetime unemployment, a secure border, and the Operation Warp Speed COVID-19 vaccine. Or consider how much energy was invested in vilifying Trump for the January 6 fiasco when compared to the several-month post-George Floyd riots, which in addition to prompting a mob attack on the White House, caused 35 deaths, $2 billion in damage, about 1,500 injured officers. Trump Derangement Syndrome is real.

Given the forces arrayed against him, how could a seemingly politically impotent Trump have any chance of a resurgent campaign? Hanson lists several critical sources for this political resurrection.
